analysis.one_liner: Ends federal tax credits that subsidize using captured carbon dioxide to pump more oil out of the ground.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in March 2026 with 12 cosponsors, all Democrats, and was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, where it has had no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, companies that capture carbon dioxide can collect a federal tax credit and then sell that CO2 to oil producers, who inject it into aging wells to squeeze out more oil — and oil producers also get a separate tax credit for the recovery costs. This bill would end both, for any facility whose construction starts after enactment. Companies could still claim the carbon capture credit when CO2 is permanently stored underground; what ends is the subsidy tied specifically to producing more oil.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit because federal money would no longer go to tax credits tied to increased oil production. People who bear the costs of climate change also benefit to the extent that removing the EOR subsidy makes it less profitable to use captured carbon as a tool for extracting more crude oil.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and people exposed to climate costs

how_it_helps.text: It repeals the section 43 tax credit, which gives oil producers a credit equal to a percentage of their costs for enhanced oil recovery projects.

It closes the part of the 45Q carbon capture credit that pays facilities for capturing carbon dioxide and then pumping it into oil fields to push out more crude oil, for any facility whose construction begins after the bill becomes law.
The result is that federal tax dollars would no longer subsidize the use of captured carbon as a tool for increased oil production.

analysis.who_pays: Oil companies that use enhanced oil recovery would lose a dedicated tax credit, and carbon capture projects that planned to sell CO2 to those oil producers for injection would lose the ability to claim the 45Q credit for that use. To the extent that subsidy helped offset capture costs, those projects could become more expensive.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil producers and carbon capture developers

drawbacks.text: The enhanced oil recovery credits are structured as an incentive for capturing carbon dioxide, and defenders argue that without them, some carbon capture projects would be uneconomical. Ending the EOR path could slow investment in capture technology overall, including technology that might eventually be used for permanent storage.

The bill only ends the tertiary injectant credit for facilities whose construction begins after enactment, and repeals the section 43 credit prospectively, so existing enhanced oil recovery operations that rely on these credits keep their current treatment.

Because the bill leaves the rest of the 45Q carbon capture credit in place, a facility that would otherwise have sent CO2 to an oil field could shift to other qualifying uses, so the actual budget savings and emissions effect depend heavily on how operators respond.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core trade is straightforward: it saves taxpayer money and stops paying oil companies to produce more oil with captured CO2, which cuts the climate benefit of the credit. The strongest objection is that EOR can be a stepping stone for early carbon capture projects and the 45Q credit as written may not distinguish oil-bound CO2 from permanently stored CO2, so the bill could make some qualifying projects unworkable. Weighing that, the cost is a possible slowdown in some carbon capture development; the benefit is ending a subsidy that pays companies to extract more crude oil. Most of the public subsidy for genuinely permanent carbon storage is left intact, which limits the bill's downside but also limits how much money it actually saves.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Ways and Means Committee right after introduction and has sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 26, 2026 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
The full action history shows no other step: no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action.
It has 12 cosponsors, all of them Democrats, and no Republican support on the committee of jurisdiction.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The oil producers and carbon capture operators that currently collect enhanced oil recovery credits are better off so far, because the credits remain untouched while the bill sits unused in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil producers who keep the credits, for now

for.name: Rep. Ro Khanna
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to end the enhanced oil recovery tax credits.

for.name: 12 Democratic cosponsors including Reps. Tlaib, Barragan, Norton, Jayapal, Frost, Ramirez, Schakowsky, and Mullin
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors of the bill.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred — no hearing, no markup, no vote to move it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 12 cosponsors are Democrats, with no Republicans signed on; the bill's fate now rests with the Ways and Means Committee, which has taken no action.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers using enhanced oil recovery
industries.note: The bill repeals their section 43 enhanced oil recovery tax credit and closes the 45Q pathway that pays them for using captured CO2 to produce more oil. Ordinary taxpayers would stop funding a subsidy tied to increased crude output.

The bill leaves the 45Q credit intact for CO2 that is permanently stored underground, but eliminates the credit for CO2 used as a tertiary injectant in oil fields. Capture projects built around selling CO2 to oil producers would lose their federal subsidy.

analysis.trajectory: Bills to repeal specific tax expenditures that sit in the Ways and Means Committee with no hearing and no action, and with no cosponsors from the majority party, rarely reach the floor. Unless leadership schedules a markup or the bill is folded into a broader tax package, it will most likely die in committee when this Congress ends in January 2027.
